newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD facing new rifts after savvy Kohl move.
newsitem.headline: German SPD facing new rifts after savvy Kohl move.

text.p: Germany's Social Democrats were caught flat-footed by conservative Chancellor Helmut Kohl's decision last week to seek an unprecedented fifth term, and the opposition party began to unravel in disputes over its own leadership.
Many SPD politicians and their labour union allies urged the party to select a challenger quickly to stand against Kohl, who handily defeated the last four opponents the SPD put forward.
SPD leaders tried to turn a deaf ear and stick to their plan to wait until April next year before naming their man for the election expected the following October.

"We cannot wait until next April to nominate our candidate," argued Christoph Grimm, a senior SPD official in Rheinland-Palatinate and president of the state parliament. "The political pressure will be too enormous to hold to that schedule."

Kohl had not been expected to announce his intentions until later in the year. But his pronouncement on Thursday that he will seek a fifth term caught the SPD completely off guard, which many political analysts said was a primary reason behind the timing.
It was a savvy move by the wily chancellor and reopened rifts in the SPD, which had fought many fractious battles before Oskar Lafontaine took control in late 1995, creating a semblance of unity.
"Whether the SPD leaders were surprised or not by Kohl's decision, their hand has now definitely been forced by the move," said Welt am Sonntag in a commentary on Sunday.
"It is now highly unlikely the SPD will be able to wait, as they intended, until April of next year," the newspaper said.

Especially if Tony Blair were to score a big win as expected for the Labour Party in Britain's election next month, "pressure on the SPD will become immense to quickly nominate a powerful figure of their own," Welt am Sonntag said.

Opinion polls conducted just before Kohl's announcement showed his Christian Democrats badly trailing the SPD. The Forsa polling institute published a survey on April 3 showing the SPD with 40 percent of the vote compared to 34 percent for Kohl's CDU and their Bavarian sister party, the CSU.
Kohl and his CDU have slumped in surveys because of a stagnating economy and record 12.2 percent unemployment.
Many polls show that Kohl could still defeat Lafontaine, but not Gerhard Schroeder, the telegenic pro-business state premier of Lower Saxony.
Lafontaine has remained silent since Kohl's announcement. Schroeder said he prefers a choice next April.
An Emnid survey to be published in Der Spiegel weekly on Monday shows 62 percent of those surveyed want to see Schroeder run against Kohl compared to 27 percent who favour Lafontaine.

"It will not be any easier for a SPD candidate if he is asked to win a race against Kohl at the last minute," said Roland Issen, head of the DAG white-collar union. "The SPD must put up an alternative to Kohl now, not some time in the future."

Gerd Andres, an SPD member of parliament and spokesman for the party's conservative "Seeheim Circle" which is close to labour unions, urged the SPD leaders to change their stance and nominate the party's candidate by December at the latest.

"The SPD will not be able to withstand another full year a debate over who will be its chancellor candidate," Andres said. "The man with the best chances has to be nominated and that is clearly Gerhard Schroeder."
But Rudolf Scharping, SPD parliamentary leader whom Kohl beat in 1994, said the party should wait until the "right time" to name its nominee.
"Kohl's announcement has not changed a thing," he told the tabloid Bild .
